discovery.question: Two partners put in equal capital but one works full-time in the firm and the other never shows up. The deed is silent. At year end, who gets what?
options: Profits are shared equally — no deed clause means equal split
The working partner gets a salary first, then equal split
The working partner gets everything
Split by capital contributed only
discovery.answer: Profits are shared equally — no deed clause means equal split
discovery.hook: Under the Partnership Act 1932, silence in the deed means equal shares — however unfair it feels. Interest on capital and partner salary exist only if the deed says so.

c12_acc_ch01.mission: Rebuild the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account — charge interest on drawings, credit interest on capital, then split the residue.
c12_acc_ch01.finale: A partnership deed is a contract, not a courtesy. Nail appropriation vs charge and the guarantees question, and this is the most bankable chapter in Accountancy.
c12_acc_ch01.subtitle: Draft the deed, then run the appropriation account.
c12_acc_ch01.role: the firm's accountant closing the year's books
c12_acc_ch01.intro: Three friends ran a design studio for a year on a handshake deal. Now they disagree about everything.
c12_acc_ch01.goal: Correctly apply deed clauses for interest on capital, interest on drawings, salary, and profit-sharing — and state the default rules when the deed is silent.

discovery.question: A new partner pays Rs 50,000 for a 1/4 share in a firm whose books show net assets worth far less. What is she really buying?
options: The firm's unrecorded goodwill
A discount on the firm's assets
A loan to the old partners
Her share of last year's profit
discovery.hook: When a firm is worth more than its books admit, the difference is goodwill — and the new partner must compensate the sacrificers in their sacrificing ratio.

c12_acc_ch02.mission: Admit the new partner — compute sacrificing ratio, value goodwill, revalue the assets, and rebuild the balance sheet.
c12_acc_ch02.finale: Admission is a negotiation written in ledger entries. Sacrificing ratio, goodwill valuation, and revaluation are the three moves examiners test every single year.
c12_acc_ch02.subtitle: Price the goodwill, split the sacrifice, restate the firm.
c12_acc_ch02.role: the valuer brought in to set the new partner's entry price
c12_acc_ch02.intro: The firm is doing well and a fourth partner wants in — but nobody agrees what the firm's reputation is worth.
c12_acc_ch02.goal: Compute new and sacrificing ratios, value and account for goodwill, pass revaluation entries, and adjust capitals on admission.

discovery.question: A partner retires mid-year and dies before his dues are settled. His executor demands the firm's entire profit for the year. What is the estate actually owed?
options: His capital, share of profit till date of death, goodwill share, and revaluation share
The whole year's profit
Only his capital balance
Whatever the remaining partners decide
discovery.answer: His capital, share of profit till date of death, goodwill share, and revaluation share
discovery.hook: Retirement reverses admission: the remaining partners gain, so they compensate the leaver in the gaining ratio — and profit accrues only up to the date of exit.

c12_acc_ch03.mission: Settle the retiring partner's account — gaining ratio, goodwill, revaluation, and the loan account if the firm can't pay at once.
c12_acc_ch03.finale: Exit accounting is admission in a mirror. Master gaining ratio and the executor's account — board questions love the death-of-partner twist.
c12_acc_ch03.subtitle: Compute the leaver's dues and the gainers' bill.
c12_acc_ch03.role: the executor's accountant auditing the settlement
c12_acc_ch03.intro: A founding partner walks away — and everyone is arguing over what her share of the firm's name is worth.
c12_acc_ch03.goal: Compute gaining ratio, treat goodwill and revaluation on exit, calculate profit share to the date of exit, and prepare the retiring/deceased partner's account.

discovery.question: The firm shuts down. Creditors want Rs 3 lakh, but selling all assets fetches only Rs 2.4 lakh — and one partner is personally broke. Who absorbs the loss?
options: Partners share the deficit in profit-sharing ratio; a solvent partner may bear an insolvent partner's share
Creditors must write off the shortfall entirely
The insolvent partner's family must pay
Loss is split equally regardless of ratio
discovery.answer: Partners share the deficit in profit-sharing ratio; a solvent partner may bear an insolvent partner's share
discovery.hook: Dissolution follows a strict pecking order — outside creditors first, then partners' loans, then capitals — and an insolvent partner's deficiency falls on the solvent ones.

c12_acc_ch04.mission: Wind the firm up — open the Realisation Account, sell every asset, pay every claimant in legal order, and close the capitals.
c12_acc_ch04.finale: Dissolution is the firm's last exam: assets to cash, cash to claimants, order of payment non-negotiable. Get the Realisation Account right and the chapter is yours.
c12_acc_ch04.subtitle: Sell, settle, and shut the books in legal order.
c12_acc_ch04.role: the liquidator appointed to wind up the firm
c12_acc_ch04.intro: The partners have voted to close shop. Everything must become cash, and every rupee of cash has a legal queue.
c12_acc_ch04.goal: Distinguish dissolution of partnership from dissolution of firm, prepare the Realisation Account, and apply the correct order of settlement including insolvency.

discovery.question: A company offers shares at Rs 110 each (face value Rs 100) and 40,000 people apply for 25,000 shares. Where does the extra Rs 10 per share go, and who gets the shares?
options: The Rs 10 is securities premium; shares are allotted pro-rata
The Rs 10 is profit paid to promoters; first-come gets shares
The extra is returned; shares go to the biggest applicants
It becomes share capital; allotment is by lottery only
discovery.answer: The Rs 10 is securities premium; shares are allotted pro-rata
discovery.hook: Face value is a legal fiction — premium rides on top, oversubscription forces pro-rata allotment, and every call money irregularity lands in Calls-in-Arrears.

c12_acc_ch05.mission: Issue 1,00,000 shares at a premium — handle oversubscription, pro-rata allotment, calls-in-arrears, and a forfeiture.
c12_acc_ch05.finale: Share capital is how strangers become owners. Premium accounting, pro-rata, and forfeiture entries are the board's favourite three-step sequence.
c12_acc_ch05.subtitle: Run a share issue from application money to forfeiture.
c12_acc_ch05.role: the company secretary executing an IPO-style allotment
c12_acc_ch05.intro: A growing company needs capital and thousands of applicants want a piece — your job is to allocate it lawfully.
c12_acc_ch05.goal: Account for issue of shares at par and premium, pro-rata allotment, calls in arrears and advance, and forfeiture and reissue of shares.

discovery.question: A company borrows Rs 50 lakh by issuing debentures and offers them as a 'collateral security' for a bank loan instead of selling them. Do the debentures appear in the books?
options: No journal entry for collateral issue — it's disclosed as a note
Full issue entries must be passed
They're recorded as equity
They're recorded only when the loan defaults
discovery.answer: No journal entry for collateral issue — it's disclosed as a note
discovery.hook: Debentures are borrowed capital with a fixed promise — the quirks (collateral, discount write-off, redemption reserve) are exactly where the exam marks hide.

c12_acc_ch06.mission: Issue and redeem a debenture series — record issue at discount, write it off, build the redemption reserve, and pay the holders.
c12_acc_ch06.finale: Debenture holders are creditors, not owners — they get paid even in loss years. Know issue, redemption sources, and collateral treatment cold.
c12_acc_ch06.subtitle: Borrow against debentures, then pay them off on schedule.
c12_acc_ch06.role: the treasurer managing the company's long-term borrowings
c12_acc_ch06.intro: The company needs Rs 50 lakh for expansion but doesn't want to dilute ownership — so it borrows from the public.
c12_acc_ch06.goal: Account for debenture issue at par/premium/discount, collateral security, interest treatment, and redemption including Debenture Redemption Reserve.

discovery.question: A company's accountant parks 'loans repayable in 5 years' under current liabilities to make the balance sheet look shorter. Under Schedule III, what went wrong?
options: Long-term borrowings must sit under non-current liabilities — classification is mandated, not cosmetic
Nothing — presentation is the accountant's choice
It should be under provisions
It should be netted against reserves
discovery.answer: Long-term borrowings must sit under non-current liabilities — classification is mandated, not cosmetic
discovery.hook: Schedule III of the Companies Act fixes the shape of every line item — financial statements are historical, monetary records presented in a legally prescribed form.

c12_acc_ch07.mission: Draft the company's Statement of Profit and Loss and Balance Sheet in Schedule III form — every item in its prescribed line.
c12_acc_ch07.finale: A company's accounts are a legal document, not a scrapbook. Learn the Schedule III map and every later chapter — ratios, cash flow — gets easier.
c12_acc_ch07.subtitle: Assemble statutory financial statements, line by line.
c12_acc_ch07.role: the chartered accountant signing off the annual report
c12_acc_ch07.intro: Year-end at a listed company: every figure must land on its legally assigned line before the board meeting.
c12_acc_ch07.goal: Prepare the Statement of Profit and Loss and Balance Sheet per Schedule III, correctly classifying items as current/non-current, equity, borrowings, and provisions.

discovery.question: Two companies report identical profits. One has current ratio 0.9 and debt-equity 3:1, the other 2.1 and 0.5:1. Same profit — which would you lend to?
options: The second — liquidity and gearing say it can actually pay you back
The first — high debt means high ambition
Neither — profit is the only number that matters
Whichever has higher revenue
discovery.answer: The second — liquidity and gearing say it can actually pay you back
discovery.hook: Profit is an opinion until ratios cross-examine it — liquidity, solvency, activity, and profitability ratios each answer a different survival question.

c12_acc_ch08.mission: Run a full ratio autopsy — compute liquidity, solvency, turnover, and profitability ratios and defend your verdict on the firm.
c12_acc_ch08.finale: Analysis turns statements into evidence. Ratio interpretation — not just computation — is what separates a 90 from a 70 in this chapter.
c12_acc_ch08.subtitle: Cross-examine the statements with ratios and common-size analysis.
c12_acc_ch08.role: a credit analyst deciding whether to lend
c12_acc_ch08.intro: A bank's loan committee hands you two sets of financial statements and one hour to pick the safer bet.
c12_acc_ch08.goal: Compute and interpret liquidity, solvency, activity, and profitability ratios, and prepare comparative and common-size statements.

discovery.question: A firm shows Rs 8 lakh profit but its bank balance fell all year and it nearly defaulted on rent. How can profit rise while cash vanishes?
options: Profit is accrual-based — credit sales, depreciation, and asset purchases move cash differently than income
The accountant must have made an error
Cash always follows profit within a year
The firm must be hiding money
discovery.answer: Profit is accrual-based — credit sales, depreciation, and asset purchases move cash differently than income
discovery.hook: Profit and cash are strangers — the cash flow statement reconciles them by sorting every rupee into operating, investing, and financing buckets.

c12_acc_ch09.mission: Build the Cash Flow Statement — strip non-cash items, sort flows into operating, investing, and financing, and reconcile the cash balance.
c12_acc_ch09.finale: Cash is the fact, profit is the story. Under AS-3's three-activity grid, you can finally see where the money actually went — a skill auditors and analysts use daily.
c12_acc_ch09.subtitle: Trace where cash truly flowed under AS-3.
c12_acc_ch09.role: the forensic accountant tracing the missing cash
c12_acc_ch09.intro: Profitable on paper, broke in the bank — your job is to show the directors exactly where the cash went.
c12_acc_ch09.goal: Classify transactions into operating, investing, and financing activities and prepare a cash flow statement by the indirect method.

discovery.question: A single amoeba divides into two and the 'parent' vanishes — while a mango tree flowers for decades before it dies. Which organism is 'immortal', and does reproduction even need death?
options: Asexual single-celled forms have no natural death — the parent literally becomes the offspring
The tree is immortal because it lives longer
Neither — all organisms die before reproducing
Amoeba dies; only the division products survive
discovery.answer: Asexual single-celled forms have no natural death — the parent literally becomes the offspring
discovery.hook: In binary fission there is no corpse — the parent IS the offspring. Reproduction maintains the species, not the individual, and life span is whatever happens between birth and reproduction's end.

c12_bio_ch01.mission: Sort a wall of organisms by reproductive strategy — fission, budding, fragmentation, vegetative propagules — then trace where sex raised the stakes.
c12_bio_ch01.finale: Asexual speed versus sexual variety — every later chapter (flowers, humans, genetics) is this trade-off played at higher resolution. NEET asks it every year.
c12_bio_ch01.subtitle: Compare the world's two ways of making more life.
c12_bio_ch01.role: a field biologist cataloguing reproduction strategies
c12_bio_ch01.intro: From a dividing amoeba to a flowering mango — your job is to map how every organism copies itself.
c12_bio_ch01.goal: Distinguish asexual and sexual reproduction, identify vegetative propagules, and explain why sexual reproduction persists despite its cost.

discovery.question: An apple seed you plant grows into a tree whose apples taste nothing like the parent's — yet the orange trees from seedless-orange cuttings are identical. What did the seed scramble that the cutting didn't?
options: Fertilisation shuffled two parents' genes; the cutting skipped meiosis entirely
Seeds always mutate; cuttings never do
Apple DNA is unstable, orange DNA is stable
The seed's food store altered the fruit
discovery.answer: Fertilisation shuffled two parents' genes; the cutting skipped meiosis entirely
discovery.hook: Double fertilisation makes every seed a genetic lottery ticket — which is why orchards clone and breeders cross. Pollination is just delivery; the fusion is the event.

c12_bio_ch02.mission: Follow one pollen grain — from anther to stigma, down the tube, through double fertilisation, to a seed and fruit.
c12_bio_ch02.finale: Two fusions in one ovule — zygote plus endosperm — is the trick that feeds every seed on Earth. Diagrams of this chapter are guaranteed marks in boards and NEET.
c12_bio_ch02.subtitle: Trace pollen to seed through the flower's double fusion.
c12_bio_ch02.role: a plant breeder designing next season's cross
c12_bio_ch02.intro: Inside a single flower, two male gametes are racing toward two different targets — control the race and you control the harvest.
c12_bio_ch02.goal: Describe micro- and megasporogenesis, pollination types, double fertilisation, and post-fertilisation changes including apomixis and polyembryony.

discovery.question: A human male releases about 300 million sperm per ejaculate, but a female releases roughly one ovum a month — yet fertilisation fails more often than it succeeds. Why does biology bother with such asymmetry?
options: Sperm are cheap, motile competitors; the ovum is a rare, resource-rich target — selection runs on the race
It's a design flaw with no purpose
Most sperm are defective by default
The numbers are actually equal in healthy adults
discovery.answer: Sperm are cheap, motile competitors; the ovum is a rare, resource-rich target — selection runs on the race
discovery.hook: Gametogenesis runs two opposite strategies — mass production versus monthly investment — and the menstrual cycle exists to time the entire rendezvous.

c12_bio_ch03.mission: Escort one sperm through every barrier — epididymis, tract, zona pellucida — then track the zygote to implantation and beyond.
c12_bio_ch03.finale: From seminiferous tubule to placenta in one connected pipeline — this is the highest-weightage chapter in the unit. Know the cycle hormones and the journey earns itself.
c12_bio_ch03.subtitle: Run the full pipeline from gamete to newborn.
c12_bio_ch03.role: an embryologist narrating fertilisation for a fertility clinic
c12_bio_ch03.intro: One cell must survive the hardest journey in human biology, and the uterus must be ready exactly when it arrives.
c12_bio_ch03.goal: Explain gametogenesis in both sexes, the menstrual cycle's hormonal control, fertilisation, implantation, gestation, parturition, and lactation.

discovery.question: A couple uses an IUD and never misses a dose of anything — yet a friend who relied on the 'safe period' conceived. Both are contraception; why did one fail?
options: IUDs physically prevent implantation; the rhythm method bets on predicting an ovulation that biology can shift
IUDs are hormones, rhythm is a barrier
The rhythm method works only after age 30
IUDs kill sperm chemically
discovery.answer: IUDs physically prevent implantation; the rhythm method bets on predicting an ovulation that biology can shift
discovery.hook: Every contraceptive attacks a different link — ovulation, sperm-egg meeting, or implantation — and reliability tracks how hard that link is to break.

c12_bio_ch04.mission: Match each contraceptive to the exact step it blocks — then advise three couples with three different needs.
c12_bio_ch04.finale: Reproductive health is applied reproductive biology — the same hormones and anatomy from last chapter, pointed at real decisions. Expect an assertion-reason on contraceptive mechanisms.
c12_bio_ch04.subtitle: Map every contraceptive to the step it interrupts.
c12_bio_ch04.role: a public-health counsellor advising a family clinic
c12_bio_ch04.intro: Three couples, three different situations — pick the method that actually matches the biology.
c12_bio_ch04.goal: Classify contraceptive methods by mechanism, identify common STIs and their prevention, and explain infertility treatments including IVF and related ART.

discovery.question: A colour-blind father and a normal-vision mother have a son. The son is colour-blind — but he got his Y from his father, not his X. Whose chromosome betrayed him?
options: The mother's — she was a carrier, and sons get X only from her
The father's Y carried the allele
A new mutation, guaranteed
The question is impossible — traits come from fathers
discovery.answer: The mother's — she was a carrier, and sons get X only from her
discovery.hook: Criss-cross inheritance: father passes X-linked traits to daughters, who pass them to sons. Mendel's ratios still rule — sex just rigged which parent hands over the allele.

c12_bio_ch05.mission: Run Mendel's crosses — monohybrid, dihybrid, then break his law with linkage, blood groups, and a pedigree puzzle.
c12_bio_ch05.finale: Nine phenotypes, three laws, one chromosome map — genetics is the most mathematical chapter in biology and the most predictive. Master the crosses and the pedigree solves itself.
c12_bio_ch05.subtitle: Predict offspring from Mendel's laws to pedigrees.
c12_bio_ch05.role: a genetic counsellor reading a family pedigree
c12_bio_ch05.intro: A family wants to know why a trait skipped a generation and struck the grandson — the pedigree holds the answer.
c12_bio_ch05.goal: Apply Mendel's laws, explain incomplete dominance, codominance, linkage, sex determination and sex-linked inheritance, and analyse pedigrees.

discovery.question: Your DNA is identical in every cell — yet a liver cell is nothing like a neuron. How?
options: Different genes are switched on in each cell type
Each cell type has different DNA sequences
Neurons lose their DNA after forming
Liver cells mutate faster
discovery.answer: Different genes are switched on in each cell type
discovery.hook: Same book, different pages read. Unzip the helix and see which base pairs make replication, transcription, and translation possible.

c12_bio_ch06.mission: Unzip the helix past 70% — which pairs break first?
c12_bio_ch06.finale: Replication, transcription, translation — the molecule that makes you, you. This is the chapter biology was building toward since class 6.
c12_bio_ch06.subtitle: Copy the code, transcribe a gene, translate a protein.
c12_bio_ch06.role: a molecular biologist inside the nucleus
c12_bio_ch06.intro: Griffith's mice, Hershey-Chase's blender, Watson-Crick's helix — follow the evidence that proved DNA runs the cell.
c12_bio_ch06.goal: Explain DNA structure and packaging, semi-conservative replication, transcription, genetic code, translation, lac operon regulation, and DNA fingerprinting.

discovery.question: In a population, 36% of people can't roll their tongue — a recessive trait. If the population obeys Hardy-Weinberg, what fraction are carriers — and what would break the equilibrium?
options: 48% are carriers; migration, selection, drift, or non-random mating break equilibrium
64% are carriers; only mutation breaks it
36% are carriers; nothing can break it
Cannot be computed from recessive frequency
discovery.answer: 48% are carriers; migration, selection, drift, or non-random mating break equilibrium
discovery.hook: p + q = 1 lets you see hidden carriers — and any force that shifts allele frequencies IS evolution happening in real time.

c12_bio_ch07.mission: Test evolution's engine — compute allele frequencies, disturb the equilibrium, and watch a population drift toward speciation.
c12_bio_ch07.finale: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies — everything else (Darwin, fossils, homologous limbs, human origins) is evidence for that single mechanism.
c12_bio_ch07.subtitle: Measure evolution itself with allele frequencies.
c12_bio_ch07.role: a population geneticist tracking a species in flux
c12_bio_ch07.intro: From Miller's sparking flask to Darwin's finches — your job is to test whether allele frequencies are actually moving.
c12_bio_ch07.goal: Explain the origin of life, evidences and mechanisms of evolution, apply Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and outline human evolution.

discovery.question: A malaria patient has fevers that spike every 3-4 days like clockwork — while a typhoid patient's fever never truly leaves. Why does one disease pulse and the other persist?
options: Plasmodium bursts RBCs in synchronised cycles; Salmonella hides inside cells continuously
Malaria bacteria divide daily; typhoid is viral
The immune system only fights malaria on schedule
Fever timing is random in both
discovery.answer: Plasmodium bursts RBCs in synchronised cycles; Salmonella hides inside cells continuously
discovery.hook: Each pathogen's life cycle writes its symptom timetable — know the organism and you can read the disease off the patient's chart.

c12_bio_ch08.mission: Diagnose the ward — match typhoid, malaria, pneumonia, and the rest to their agents, then deploy innate and acquired immunity.
c12_bio_ch08.finale: Pathogen life cycle, immune response, intervention — medicine is this chapter industrialised. Widal test, sporozoites, and antibody types are guaranteed NEET/board material.
c12_bio_ch08.subtitle: Match pathogens to symptoms, then fire the immune system.
c12_bio_ch08.role: a doctor working the infectious-disease ward
c12_bio_ch08.intro: Five patients, five fevers — read each disease's signature and decide where the immune system needs backup.
c12_bio_ch08.goal: Link each disease to its pathogen and transmission, explain innate and acquired immunity, vaccination, AIDS, cancer, and the effects of drugs and alcohol.

discovery.question: A dairy's best buffalo gives 12 litres a day; the herd average is 4. The owner breeds her to a random good bull and the daughters average just 6. Where did the milk genes go?
options: Her superiority was partly environmental and her allele luck broke at meiosis — outcrossing can't clone a phenotype
The bull was defective
Daughters inherit nothing from mothers
Milk yield isn't genetic at all
discovery.answer: Her superiority was partly environmental and her allele luck broke at meiosis — outcrossing can't clone a phenotype
discovery.hook: Breeding is managed meiosis — you can stack the deck with selection, inbreeding, and MOET, but fertilisation still shuffles the hand.

c12_bio_ch09.mission: Design the improvement program — choose inbreeding, outcrossing, or hybridisation, then run the same logic on crop varieties.
c12_bio_ch09.finale: Green Revolution to MOET — feeding a billion people is applied genetics. Breed types, biofortification, and single-cell protein close the loop for boards.
c12_bio_ch09.subtitle: Breed better herds and harvests by steering meiosis.
c12_bio_ch09.role: an animal breeder running a livestock improvement program
c12_bio_ch09.intro: The herd is average, the market isn't — pick the mating strategy that moves the mean.
c12_bio_ch09.goal: Differentiate inbreeding, outbreeding, and cross-breeding; explain MOET, plant breeding for disease resistance, biofortification, and single-cell protein.
